source_read: PDF (version of record), Academic Emergency Medicine 7(8), pp. 873-877, all 5 pages; text layer extracted with pdftotext -layout and every number used below checked on 150-dpi renderings of each page (Tables 1-3 on pp. 874-875; no figures).

claims.overstatement: One clause goes beyond the source: 'all of which would tend to raise the share'. The source gives no direction for any of these case-finding features; the editors' inference is reasonable for the review of every chart coded for infarction (p. 876) and for leaving out the 9 patients discharged from the ED (15 of 259 would be 5.8%), but not for the urine-testing policy. The authors' own concern about that policy is that older patients (over 50) who had used cocaine may not have been captured (pp. 876-877); older patients carry more coronary risk, so missing them would, if anything, lower the share. Suggest: 'some of which would tend to raise the share, while the urine-testing policy may have missed older patients'. Minor: the paper names the setting only as an urban university-affiliated trauma centre; Flint, Michigan comes from the authors' department and correspondence address (Hurley Medical Center, p. 873), which is a fair reading. No causal language from this source; the claim correctly says no comparison group of patients without cocaine use exists.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude that comes from Weber et al. checks on the rendered pages: 15 of 250 (6%); 95% CI 3.1-8.9% in the Results (p. 875) and 4.1-8.9% in the abstract (p. 873); 185 of 196 urine screens positive; mean age 33.5; men 77%; African American 84%; tobacco 77%; 9 ED discharges excluded; 7 complication events (2 sustained VT, 3 SVT, 1 heart failure, 1 bradydysrhythmia), none after 12 hours; all 250 alive at discharge; Kontos et al. 2.5% of 241; retrospective series 0-31%. Editors' calculations recomputed: exact (Clopper-Pearson) 95% CI for 15/250 = 3.40-9.70% (same as the claim); the printed Results interval is the normal-approximation interval (3.06-8.94%); the abstract's 4.1% matches no standard method (Wilson gives 3.67-9.66%); 0 events after 12 hours in 250 patients gives an exact two-sided 95% upper limit of 1.46% (claim: 1.5%, same). 'Most had used cocaine within the previous 24 hours, mostly by smoking crack' holds on either version (77% abstract / 78% Results; crack 85% abstract / 91% Results). The 7 complications are events; the paper does not say they were in 7 different patients, so 'in 2 patients ... in 3 ...' is right but they should not be summed into a patient count. A qualifying point from this source for the claim's ECG sentence: in this series 13 of the 15 infarctions (87%, exact 95% CI 59.5-98.3%; editors' calculation) had an initial ECG consistent with infarction (9) or showing ischaemic changes (4), and about 12 of the 235 patients without infarction had an ischaemic or infarct-suggestive ECG (25 such ECGs overall minus 13; specificity about 95%, editors' calculation) - far above the 36% sensitivity the claim cites second-hand for COCHPA. The 36% is therefore a single study's figure and the claim might say so (e.g. 'in COCHPA, ... while in the Flint series 13 of 15 infarctions had ischaemic or infarct changes on the first ECG'). Design: the Methods call it a retrospective cohort study (p. 873), the Discussion a retrospective case series (p. 876); no comparison group. The last author (J. E. Hollander) also led COCHPA and the 29-hospital series, so the 6% here and COCHPA's 6% come from overlapping investigators (not independent replication in the METHODS §6.3 sense).

anchors.locator: Methods › Study Setting and Population, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Urban university-affiliated trauma centre, annual ED census 55,000 (authors' department: Hurley Medical Center, Flint, MI, footnote p. 873). Departmental policy during the study: all ED faculty admit every patient with cocaine-associated chest pain for at least 23 hours. Computer-assisted records search of ED presentations 1 July 1996 to 28 February 1998, crossing ICD-9 codes for chest pain and myocardial infarction with codes for cocaine and/or drug abuse; list checked against an ED log of all admitted patients. Entry: documented cocaine use in the week before presentation or urine positive for cocaine or metabolites; chief complaint of anterior, precordial or left-sided chest discomfort for less than 12 hours; age 18 or over.

Cardiac isoenzymes in all patients on presentation and then every 8 hours for a total of 24 hours. Infarction defined by WHO criteria: CK-MB at least twice the institutional normal value with a typical rise and fall; infarcts classed as Q-wave or non-Q-wave and by ECG location.

259 patients with cocaine-associated chest pain identified; 9 were discharged from the ED despite the admission protocol and excluded; 250 formed the study group. The 9 did not differ significantly in age, sex, ethnicity or cardiac risk factors; their later complications are unknown; all 9 were alive at the end of the study period.

Mean age 33.5 years (SD 8.5); men 192 (77%); African American 208 (84%), White 24 (10%), Hispanic 3 (1%), other/unknown 15 (6%); hypertension 64 (26%); hypercholesterolaemia 21 (8%); family history 86 (34%); diabetes 14 (6%); tobacco use 192 (77%); previous chest pain 100 (40%); previous myocardial infarction 16 (6%). The Discussion gives men as 76% (p. 877); 192/250 = 76.8%.

All patients reported cocaine use within 7 days or had cocaine metabolites in urine; precise history available for all but 3. Last use within 24 hours in 193 (78%) and within 4 hours in 57 (22%) (the two add to 250 and 100%). Urine toxicology done in 196, positive in 185 (94%). Crack inhalation the commonest route (91%). Abstract (p. 873): 77% within 24 hours; crack 85%, intravenous 2%, nasal 6%.

250 patients, mean age 33.5 (SD 8.5); 77% men; 84% African American; 185 of 196 tested had cocaine or metabolites in urine (94%); tobacco 77%; 77% used cocaine in the preceding 24 hours; 25 (10%) had ECG evidence of ischaemia; AMI in 15 (6%) with 95% CI printed 4.1% to 8.9% (WHO criteria); complications bradydysrhythmia 0.4%, heart failure 0.4%, SVT 1.2%, sustained VT 0.8%.

Myocardial infarction in 15 of 250 (6%), 95% CI printed 3.1% to 8.9%. Initial ECG consistent with AMI in 9, ischaemic changes in 4, normal or nondiagnostic in 2. Every patient with AMI had at least one CK-MB above twice the upper limit of normal and met WHO criteria; 8 anterior, 6 inferior, 1 indeterminate; 9 Q-wave (60%). Recomputed (editors' calculation): exact 95% CI 3.40-9.70%; the printed interval equals the normal-approximation interval (3.06-8.94%).

24 patients first admitted to the coronary care unit (stay 2.7, SD 1.9 days); mean hospital stay 2.2 (SD 2.0) days; all 250 survived to discharge. Complications: bradydysrhythmia 1 (0.4%), heart failure 1 (0.4%), SVT 3 (1.2%), sustained VT 2 (0.8%); none occurred more than 12 hours after ED arrival (p. 876). Recomputed: 0 of 250 after 12 hours, exact 95% upper limit 1.46%.

Initial ECG in all 250: normal 67 (27%), nonspecific 125 (50%), abnormal nondiagnostic 33 (13%), old ischaemia 6 (2%), ischaemia not known to be old 10 (4%), suggestive of AMI 9 (4%); 25 with ischaemic or infarct-suggestive ECGs. Among the 15 infarctions, 9 had an AMI-consistent and 4 an ischaemic initial ECG. Editors' calculation: 13 of 15 infarctions (87%; exact 95% CI 59.5-98.3%) had ischaemic or infarct changes on the first ECG; about 12 of 235 without infarction did (specificity about 95%).

Retrospective studies found AMI in 0% to 31% of patients with cocaine-associated chest pain; earlier estimates limited by selection bias; two prospective studies found 5-6%. Examples: 3 of 48 coronary-care patients (6%); 0 of 101 in monitored beds (47 of them with incomplete marker testing); 22 of 70 admitted patients (31%) in a study that did not enrol patients discharged from the ED.
Prospective study: 8 of 42 patients (19%) with normal or nonspecific ECGs had elevated cardiac markers, but only 5% met WHO criteria for AMI (convenience sample; ischaemic ECGs excluded).

COCHPA: prospective, six municipal hospitals, enrolment regardless of ED disposition, AMI 6%; criticized because some sites enrolled fewer patients than expected and capture of all eligible patients was not ensured. Kontos et al.: 6 of 69 (8.5%) coronary-care patients had AMI, 2.5% of the whole cohort of 241.

Chest pain as chief complaint was required, so patients with other ischaemic symptoms may have been missed; coding errors cannot be excluded; every chart with an ICD-9 code for AMI, with or without cocaine use, was reviewed over the study period (stated as 19 months) to limit over- or undercoding.

anchors.locator: Limitations and Future Questions, 3rd paragraph (continues on p. 877)
anchors.extracted: By departmental policy urine toxicology was part of the cardiac work-up only for patients aged 50 or under without traditional risk factors (earlier work: cocaine use in only 2% of ED chest-pain patients over 50); the authors say a small number of patients over 50 who had used cocaine may not have been captured. About 6% (11 of 196) reported use but tested negative.

Every diagnosed AMI had CK-MB above 20 IU/L, while the criterion required only twice normal (10 IU/L), so the authors cannot be certain that a very small number of non-Q-wave infarctions were not missed. Patients young, mostly men (76%), smokers (77%).

anchors.locator: Limitations and Future Questions, 5th paragraph; Conclusions
anchors.extracted: No patient had an adverse event more than 12 hours after ED arrival; the authors say this confirms an earlier suggested risk of 1.6 per 1,000 after a 12-hour observation (0 of 250 is compatible with up to 1.46%, so it cannot confirm a figure that small; editors' calculation). Conclusion: approximately 6% incidence of AMI among ED patients with cocaine-associated chest pain, said to validate COCHPA.

key_findings.correction: Exact upper limit recomputed as 1.46%. Small addition: the 7 complications are events; the paper does not say they occurred in 7 different patients.
The 3rd paragraph runs on to p. 877 (where the authors say some patients over 50 'were not captured'); by the locator convention it counts on p. 876, so the location stands.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: Wald 3.06-8.94%, exact 3.40-9.70%, Wilson 3.67-9.66%; the abstract's 4.1% matches none.
193/250 = 77.2% and 193/247 = 78.1%; the abstract and Results percentages fit different denominators, but the 193 + 57 = 250 problem stands.
As the card says, 'anterior' may include right-sided anterior pain, so this may not be an inconsistency; minor either way.
1 July 1996 to 28 February 1998 is 20 calendar months; 192/250 = 76.8%.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence is a sensible choice for a case series whose question is a proportion (METHODS §5.3 lists no instrument for case series). Domain 2 ('yes') is generous because entry depended on cocaine or drug-abuse coding, but that problem is already rated under domains 1 and 5; the overall 'moderate' summary is agreed. The card's selection_effects text correctly limits the 'tends to raise the proportion' reading to the case-finding asymmetry and the 9 exclusions and treats the urine-testing policy as a reason older patients were under-captured.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is right: the main number is reported correctly; the overreach is in 'identical', 'validates COCHPA' (shared last author) and 'confirms' 1.6 per 1,000 from 0 of 250.

missed: ECG performance in this series (editors' calculation from p. 875, Results 6th and 7th paragraphs): 13 of 15 infarctions (87%, exact 95% CI 59.5-98.3%) had an initial ECG consistent with AMI or with ischaemic changes, and about 12 of 235 without infarction had an ischaemic or infarct-suggestive ECG (specificity about 95%). The data are on the card (key finding 4), but this contrast with the 36% ECG sensitivity reported for COCHPA (used in cl_coc_chest_pain_mi) is not drawn.
About 6% of patients who reported use had negative urine toxicology: 11 of 196 tested (5.6%) (pp. 875, 877) - on the card only as '6%'; the count may help.
